item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Gloucestershire Orchard Trust (GOT)

Conserves, promotes and celebrates traditional orchards

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust (GOT) works to conserve, promote and celebrate the county's traditional orchards and their fruit varieties. We are a registered charity dedicated to preserving this important part of Gloucestershire's heritage.

Our Mission

Traditional orchards are a valuable part of our landscape and cultural heritage. They provide:

  • Habitat for wildlife including rare species
  • Heritage fruit varieties unique to Gloucestershire
  • Connection to our agricultural past
  • Community spaces for learning and enjoyment

What We Do

GOT is involved in a wide range of activities:

  • Orchard conservation - Working with landowners to protect and restore traditional orchards
  • Varietal research - Documenting and preserving Gloucestershire's heritage fruit varieties
  • Community engagement - Supporting community orchards across the county
  • Education and training - Teaching traditional orchard management skills
  • Events and celebrations - Apple Days, wassails, and other orchard events

Explore Our Resources

Visit our Apple Varieties section to learn about Gloucestershire's unique apples, browse our Perry Pears collection, or discover Gloucestershire Plums.

You can also find information about Community Orchards throughout the county.

item.title: Varietal Research
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Varietal Research

Preserving Gloucestershire's Fruit Heritage

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust is committed to identifying, documenting, and preserving the county's unique heritage fruit varieties. Our varietal research program is essential to understanding and conserving Gloucestershire's pomological heritage.

Our Research Focus

We conduct extensive research into three main categories of fruit:

  • Apples - Including dessert, culinary, and cider varieties native to or historically grown in Gloucestershire
  • Perry Pears - The traditional pears used to make perry, Gloucestershire's signature drink
  • Plums - Heritage plum varieties that have been cultivated in the county for generations

Research Methods

Our varietal research involves:

  • Orchard surveys and fruit identification
  • Historical documentation and archive research
  • DNA analysis and pomological description
  • Collaboration with national fruit collections
  • Recording oral histories from local growers

Key Publications

Our research has resulted in several important publications:

  • Native Apples of Gloucestershire (PDF)
  • Perry Pears of Gloucestershire (PDF)
  • Gloucestershire Plums (PDF)

Identification Services

We offer fruit identification services to help identify unknown varieties found in old orchards. Visit our Identification page to learn more about this service.

Browse Our Collections

Explore our documented varieties:

  • Apple Varieties
  • Perry Pear Varieties
  • Plum Varieties

item.title: Community Orchards in Gloucestershire
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Community Orchards in Gloucestershire

Bringing Communities Together Through Orchards

Community orchards are wonderful spaces that bring people together to learn, work, and celebrate traditional fruit growing. Gloucestershire is home to many thriving community orchards, and the Gloucestershire Orchard Trust supports their development and management.

What is a Community Orchard?

A community orchard is:

  • A shared green space planted with fruit trees
  • Managed by and for the local community
  • A place for learning traditional orchard skills
  • A habitat for wildlife and biodiversity
  • A space for community events and celebrations

Benefits of Community Orchards

Community orchards provide numerous benefits:

  • Social - Meeting neighbors, building community connections, intergenerational activities
  • Environmental - Creating wildlife habitat, planting trees, supporting biodiversity
  • Educational - Learning about fruit growing, tree care, seasonal cycles
  • Health & Wellbeing - Outdoor exercise, fresh air, stress reduction, access to fresh fruit
  • Cultural - Preserving heritage varieties, traditional skills, local food culture

Community Orchards Across Gloucestershire

There are community orchards throughout the county, including in:

  • Gloucester
  • Cheltenham
  • Stroud
  • Tewkesbury
  • Forest of Dean
  • Cotswolds

Starting a Community Orchard

Interested in starting a community orchard in your area? GOT can help with:

  • Site assessment and planning
  • Variety selection appropriate for your location
  • Planting advice and tree sourcing
  • Training in orchard management
  • Connecting you with other community orchards
  • Ongoing support and guidance

Get Involved

Whether you want to volunteer at an existing community orchard or start a new one, GOT can help connect you with opportunities in your area.

Community orchards often hold regular work parties, seasonal celebrations like wassails and apple days, and offer training in traditional orchard skills like grafting and pruning.

item.title: Apple Varieties
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Apple Varieties of Gloucestershire

Discovering Gloucestershire's Apple Heritage

Gloucestershire has a rich heritage of apple varieties, from dessert apples eaten fresh to culinary apples for cooking and cider apples for traditional cider making. Many of these varieties originated in the county or have been grown here for centuries.

Native Apples of Gloucestershire

Several apple varieties are native to or closely associated with Gloucestershire. These include both well-known varieties and rare heritage apples that we are working to preserve.

Download our comprehensive guide: Native Apples of Gloucestershire (PDF)

Types of Apples

Dessert Apples - Sweet, crisp apples perfect for eating fresh

Culinary Apples - Cooking apples that break down when heated, ideal for pies and sauces

Cider Apples - High tannin varieties used for traditional cider making

Dual Purpose - Versatile varieties suitable for multiple uses

Featured Gloucestershire Apple Varieties

Explore some of Gloucestershire's most important apple varieties:

  • Ashmead's Kernel - A renowned dessert apple originating from Gloucester
  • Gloucester Royal - Historic variety with strong county connections
  • Hunt's Duke of Gloucester - Named for the county
  • Eden - Heritage Gloucestershire variety
  • Councillor - Traditional local apple
  • Bedminster Pippin - Classic west country variety

Characteristics to Look For

When identifying apple varieties, consider:

  • Size and shape of the fruit
  • Skin color and texture
  • Flesh color and texture
  • Taste - sweet, sharp, aromatic
  • Season of ripening
  • Tree growth habit

Growing Heritage Apples

Heritage apple varieties are well-suited to Gloucestershire's climate and soils. Many are hardy, disease-resistant, and require less intervention than modern varieties.

If you're interested in planting heritage apple varieties, GOT can provide advice on suitable varieties for your location and intended use.

Apple Identification Service

Found an unknown apple tree in your garden or local orchard? We may be able to help identify it. Visit our Identification page for more information.

item.title: Ashmead's Kernel
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Ashmead's Kernel

A Gloucester Original

Ashmead's Kernel is one of Gloucestershire's most famous contributions to the apple world. This exceptional dessert apple originated in Gloucester around 1700 and is still highly regarded by apple enthusiasts today.

Origin and History

This variety was raised by Dr. Ashmead of Gloucester in the early 18th century. Despite its somewhat unprepossessing appearance, it has become renowned for its outstanding flavor and is considered one of the finest dessert apples.

The apple was distributed from Gloucester nurseries and gained popularity throughout England and eventually internationally. Today it's grown by apple enthusiasts worldwide who appreciate its unique taste.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium
  • Shape: Round-conical, slightly irregular
  • Skin: Greenish-yellow to golden, often with brown russet patches
  • Flesh: Cream colored, crisp and juicy
  • Flavor: Rich, aromatic, sweet-sharp with hints of pear drop

Tree Characteristics:

  • Moderately vigorous growth
  • Spreading habit
  • Good disease resistance
  • Regular cropping

Season and Use

Picking Time: Late September to October

Storage: Keeps well until January or later

Use: Excellent dessert apple, best eaten fresh. The flavor improves with storage.

Growing Notes

Ashmead's Kernel is well-suited to Gloucestershire's climate:

  • Hardy and reliable
  • Performs well in cooler climates
  • Suitable for organic growing
  • Self-fertile but crops better with a pollination partner
  • Harvest Group 4 (mid-late season)

Culinary Uses

While primarily a dessert apple, Ashmead's Kernel can also be used in:

  • Fresh eating - the primary use
  • Salads - retains crispness
  • Juice - aromatic and flavorful
  • Light cooking - though flavor is best appreciated fresh

Availability

Ashmead's Kernel trees are available from specialist fruit tree nurseries. The variety is also held in the National Fruit Collection and other heritage fruit collections.

This apple represents an important part of Gloucestershire's pomological heritage and continues to delight apple lovers more than 300 years after its origin.

item.title: Bedminster Pippin
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Bedminster Pippin

A Classic West Country Dessert Apple

Bedminster Pippin is a traditional West Country apple variety with strong connections to the Bristol and Gloucestershire area. This attractive dessert apple has been grown in the region for generations.

Origin and History

The variety is named after Bedminster, an area of Bristol that borders Gloucestershire. While the exact origin date is uncertain, it has been grown in the region since at least the 19th century.

Bedminster Pippin was once commonly found in orchards throughout the West Country but became increasingly rare in the 20th century. Efforts to preserve this heritage variety have ensured its survival.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium
  • Shape: Round to slightly conical
  • Skin: Pale yellow-green with red flush and stripes
  • Flesh: White, crisp and juicy
  • Flavor: Sweet with good balance, pleasant aromatic quality

Tree Characteristics:

  • Moderate to vigorous growth
  • Spreading habit
  • Good cropper
  • Hardy and reliable

Season and Use

Picking Time: September to early October

Storage: Keeps for several weeks to a few months

Use: Dessert apple, excellent for fresh eating

Growing Notes

Bedminster Pippin grows well in Gloucestershire conditions:

  • Well-suited to West Country climate
  • Reliable cropping
  • Reasonably disease resistant
  • Suitable for garden growing
  • Benefits from a pollination partner

Culinary Uses

This versatile apple can be used for:

  • Fresh eating - crisp and flavorful
  • Salads - attractive appearance
  • Light cooking - holds shape reasonably well
  • Juice and cider - contributes good flavor

Heritage Value

Bedminster Pippin represents an important part of the West Country's fruit growing heritage. Preserving varieties like this helps maintain genetic diversity and connects us to our regional food culture.

GOT encourages the planting and preservation of regional varieties like Bedminster Pippin as part of our mission to conserve Gloucestershire's orchard heritage.

item.title: Councillor
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Councillor

A Local Heritage Variety

Councillor is a traditional apple variety associated with Gloucestershire. This dual-purpose apple has been valued in local orchards for both eating and cooking qualities.

Origin and History

The Councillor apple has been grown in Gloucestershire for many generations. While documentation of its exact origin is limited, it represents the type of local variety that would have been found in traditional orchards throughout the county.

Like many heritage varieties, Councillor was largely forgotten during the 20th century when commercial apple production focused on a small number of standardized varieties. GOT's research has helped document and preserve this variety.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium to large
  • Shape: Round-conical
  • Skin: Green-yellow background with red flush
  • Flesh: Cream colored, moderately firm
  • Flavor: Good balance of sweet and sharp when fresh, becomes sweeter with storage

Tree Characteristics:

  • Vigorous growth
  • Spreading habit
  • Good cropper
  • Hardy variety

Season and Use

Picking Time: October

Storage: Keeps well through winter

Use: Dual-purpose - suitable for both eating fresh and cooking

Growing Notes

Councillor is well-adapted to Gloucestershire growing conditions:

  • Hardy and reliable
  • Suitable for traditional orchard conditions
  • Good cropper
  • Reasonably disease resistant
  • Benefits from a pollination partner

Culinary Uses

The dual-purpose nature of Councillor makes it versatile:

  • Fresh eating - pleasant when ripe
  • Cooking - softens well for pies and crumbles
  • Storage apple - flavor develops over time
  • Juice - good flavor contribution

Heritage Significance

Varieties like Councillor represent the diverse range of apples that sustained families and communities before the era of supermarket fruit. These local varieties were chosen for their suitability to local conditions and their ability to provide fruit over an extended season.

By preserving and growing heritage varieties like Councillor, we maintain genetic diversity and keep alive the knowledge of traditional fruit growing in Gloucestershire.

item.title: Eden
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Eden

A Gloucestershire Heritage Apple

Eden is a traditional apple variety with strong connections to Gloucestershire. This heritage variety represents the type of local apple that would have been commonly grown in the county's orchards.

Origin and History

The Eden apple has been recorded in Gloucestershire orchards for many generations. Like many local varieties, detailed historical records are limited, but the variety has been maintained through the county's traditional orchards.

These local varieties were often known by different names in different areas, and documentation was usually passed down through oral tradition among fruit growers rather than written records.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium
  • Shape: Round
  • Skin: Variable coloring, typically green-yellow with red markings
  • Flesh: White to cream, firm texture
  • Flavor: Good balance, typical of heritage varieties

Tree Characteristics:

  • Moderate vigor
  • Regular cropping
  • Hardy constitution
  • Well-adapted to local conditions

Season and Use

Picking Time: Autumn (specific timing varies by season)

Storage: Moderate keeping quality

Use: Versatile - suitable for eating fresh and cooking

Growing Notes

As a heritage Gloucestershire variety, Eden is:

  • Well-suited to local climate and soil
  • Hardy and reliable
  • Adapted to traditional orchard management
  • Generally good disease resistance
  • Benefits from traditional orchard spacing

Heritage Value

Varieties like Eden are important for several reasons:

  • Genetic Diversity - Local varieties maintain genetic variation
  • Climate Adaptation - Selected over generations for local conditions
  • Cultural Heritage - Connect us to traditional orcharding
  • Flavor Diversity - Offer tastes different from modern commercial varieties

Conservation

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust works to conserve varieties like Eden through:

  • Documentation and identification
  • Maintaining specimens in heritage orchards
  • Grafting to preserve genetic material
  • Encouraging planting in community orchards
  • Research into variety characteristics

By growing and preserving local varieties like Eden, we ensure that Gloucestershire's unique orchard heritage continues for future generations.

item.title: Gloucester Royal
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Gloucester Royal

Royalty Among Gloucestershire Apples

Gloucester Royal is a historic apple variety with strong connections to the city and county of Gloucester. This attractive dessert apple carries the county's name with pride and represents an important part of local pomological heritage.

Origin and History

As its name suggests, Gloucester Royal has royal connections and is strongly associated with the city of Gloucester. The variety dates back to at least the 19th century and was valued as both an attractive and flavorful apple.

The "Royal" designation indicates the high regard in which this variety was held, and it would have been grown in better gardens and orchards throughout the county.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium to large
  • Shape: Round to round-conical, regular shape
  • Skin: Yellow-green background with attractive red flush and stripes
  • Flesh: White, crisp and juicy
  • Flavor: Sweet with good aromatic quality, well-balanced

Tree Characteristics:

  • Moderate to vigorous growth
  • Good cropping ability
  • Spreading habit
  • Hardy and reliable

Season and Use

Picking Time: September to October

Storage: Good keeping quality, stores for several months

Use: Primarily dessert, excellent for fresh eating

Growing Notes

Gloucester Royal thrives in its home county:

  • Well-adapted to Gloucestershire conditions
  • Reliable cropper
  • Good disease resistance
  • Suitable for garden or orchard growing
  • Benefits from pollination partner
  • Attractive blossom

Culinary Uses

This versatile apple can be used for:

  • Fresh eating - excellent flavor and texture
  • Display - attractive appearance
  • Salads - crisp texture holds well
  • Light cooking - though best appreciated fresh
  • Juice - good aromatic flavor

Heritage and Cultural Significance

Gloucester Royal represents:

  • The county's proud fruit growing heritage
  • Connection to Gloucester's history
  • The quality of traditional English dessert apples
  • Regional identity and pride

Conservation Status

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust is working to ensure Gloucester Royal remains available for future generations. This involves:

  • Maintaining specimens in heritage orchards
  • Documenting variety characteristics
  • Making grafting material available
  • Promoting the variety to local growers
  • Including it in community orchard plantings

As one of the county's name-bearing varieties, Gloucester Royal holds special significance in our work to preserve Gloucestershire's orchard heritage.

item.title: Hunt's Duke of Gloucester
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Hunt's Duke of Gloucester

A Distinguished Gloucestershire Apple

Hunt's Duke of Gloucester is a fine dessert apple with strong connections to Gloucestershire. Named for the Duke of Gloucester, this variety exemplifies the quality of traditional English apples and the county's fruit growing heritage.

Origin and History

This variety was raised by Hunt, a nurseryman, and named in honor of the Duke of Gloucester. The apple dates to the 19th century and represents the tradition of naming prestigious varieties after royalty and nobility.

The variety gained recognition for its excellent eating qualities and attractive appearance, making it popular in better gardens and orchards throughout Gloucestershire and beyond.

Identification

Fruit Characteristics:

  • Size: Medium to large
  • Shape: Round-conical, regular and attractive
  • Skin: Golden yellow with red flush and streaks
  • Flesh: Creamy white, fine-textured, crisp and juicy
  • Flavor: Rich, sweet, aromatic with excellent balance

Tree Characteristics:

  • Moderate vigor
  • Good cropping
  • Spreading habit
  • Reliable performance

Season and Use

Picking Time: Late September to October

Storage: Excellent keeper, stores well into winter

Use: Dessert apple of the highest quality

Growing Notes

Hunt's Duke of Gloucester is well-suited to Gloucestershire:

  • Hardy and reliable
  • Good disease resistance
  • Performs well in the county's climate
  • Suitable for garden or orchard
  • Regular cropping
  • Benefits from pollination partner

Culinary Uses

This premium dessert apple is primarily used for:

  • Fresh eating - excellent flavor and texture
  • Display purposes - attractive appearance
  • Special occasions - a quality apple
  • Juice - aromatic and flavorful

Quality and Reputation

Hunt's Duke of Gloucester was recognized as a first-rate dessert apple:

  • Fine flavor and texture
  • Attractive appearance
  • Good keeping quality
  • Reliable cropping
  • Worthy of its noble name

Heritage Significance

This variety represents:

  • The peak of 19th century English apple breeding
  • Gloucestershire's connection to royal and noble patronage
  • The county's tradition of quality fruit production
  • Historical naming conventions for prestigious varieties

Conservation

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust values Hunt's Duke of Gloucester as an important heritage variety. We work to:

  • Maintain the variety in heritage collections
  • Document its characteristics and history
  • Make it available to growers
  • Promote awareness of this distinguished apple
  • Include it in appropriate planting schemes

As a variety bearing the county's name, Hunt's Duke of Gloucester holds special place in Gloucestershire's pomological heritage and our conservation efforts.

item.title: Fruit Identification Service
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Fruit Identification Service

Help Identifying Your Fruit Trees

Have you discovered an old fruit tree in your garden or local area and wonder what variety it might be? The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust offers fruit identification services to help identify unknown varieties.

Why Identify Fruit Varieties?

Identifying fruit varieties is important for several reasons:

  • Heritage Conservation - Unknown trees might be rare local varieties worth preserving
  • Proper Care - Knowing the variety helps with appropriate pruning and management
  • Harvest Timing - Different varieties ripen at different times
  • Best Use - Some apples are best for eating, others for cooking or cider
  • Historical Interest - Discovering the story behind old orchard trees

Our Identification Service

GOT can help identify:

  • Apple varieties (dessert, culinary, and cider)
  • Perry pear varieties
  • Plum varieties
  • Other orchard fruits

What We Need for Identification

To identify a fruit variety, we typically need:

Fruit Samples:

  • At least 3-4 representative fruits
  • Fruits should be mature (not under-ripe)
  • Include any with interesting features
  • Bring samples when in season (typically August-October for apples)

Information About the Tree:

  • Location (approximate age of tree if known)
  • Size and habit of the tree
  • Cropping characteristics
  • Any historical information

Photographs:

  • Whole fruit from different angles
  • Cross-section showing flesh and core
  • The tree (if accessible)
  • Any distinctive features

The Identification Process

Fruit identification involves:

  1. Physical Examination - Size, shape, color, skin texture, flesh characteristics
  2. Tasting - Flavor profile, acidity, sweetness, texture
  3. Reference Comparison - Comparing against known varieties
  4. Historical Research - Checking local records and nursery catalogs
  5. Expert Consultation - Working with national identification networks

What to Expect

Success Rate:

Not all fruits can be definitively identified. Many factors affect success:

  • Common commercial varieties are easiest to identify
  • Well-documented heritage varieties can usually be identified
  • Rare local varieties may be difficult
  • Some trees may be seedlings (not a named variety)
  • Hybrids or sports may be unidentifiable

Timing:

Identification takes time - sometimes requiring multiple samples from different years to be certain.

Identification Events

GOT often holds identification days during apple season (typically October) where you can bring samples. These events also feature:

  • Expert pomologists
  • Reference collections for comparison
  • Information about varieties
  • Opportunity to learn identification skills

After Identification

If your tree turns out to be a rare or significant variety:

  • We may ask permission to take grafting material
  • The tree could be recorded as part of our survey work
  • You'll receive advice on care and management
  • The variety might be added to heritage collections

Learn More

Interested in learning to identify fruit yourself? GOT offers training in pomology and fruit identification. Understanding fruit identification helps preserve our orchard heritage.

Key resources for identification:

  • Native Apples of Gloucestershire (PDF)
  • Perry Pears of Gloucestershire (PDF)
  • Gloucestershire Plums (PDF)

item.title: Perry Pear Varieties
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Perry Pear Varieties

Gloucestershire's Signature Fruit

Perry pears are the traditional pears used to make perry (pear cider), and Gloucestershire is the heartland of perry production in England. The county's unique perry pear varieties and centuries-old perry orchards are nationally significant.

What is Perry?

Perry is a traditional alcoholic beverage made from fermented pear juice, similar to cider but made from pears instead of apples. Unlike eating pears, perry pears are:

  • High in tannins (astringent taste)
  • Small to medium sized
  • Often hard and gritty when raw
  • Unsuitable for eating fresh
  • Perfect for fermentation

Perry Pear Heritage

Gloucestershire has a rich perry heritage dating back centuries:

  • Many unique varieties originated in the county
  • Traditional perry orchards with ancient trees
  • Centuries of perry-making knowledge
  • Cultural significance in local communities
  • Recognized nationally and internationally

Download our comprehensive guide: Perry Pears of Gloucestershire (PDF)

Notable Perry Pear Varieties

Gloucestershire is home to many distinctive perry pear varieties:

  • Taynton Squash - One of the most famous varieties, originated near Gloucester
  • Blakeney Red - Named for the Forest of Dean village
  • Thorn - Common in traditional orchards
  • Moorcroft - Highly regarded for perry quality
  • Malvern Hills - Regional variety
  • Barland - Historic variety
  • Stinking Bishop - Named for the famous cheese, also a perry pear

Perry Pear Trees

Perry pear trees have distinctive characteristics:

  • Very long-lived (200+ years possible)
  • Large, spreading trees at maturity
  • Deep-rooting
  • Take many years to come into full bearing
  • Remarkable resilience and longevity
  • Beautiful spring blossom

Traditional Perry Orchards

Traditional perry orchards are:

  • Composed of large, widely-spaced standard trees
  • Often grazed by livestock
  • Important wildlife habitat
  • Landscape features of historic significance
  • Priority habitat for conservation

Perry Making

Traditional perry production involves:

  1. Harvesting pears when fully ripe (often picked from the ground)
  2. Storing briefly to soften
  3. Milling or crushing the pears
  4. Pressing to extract juice
  5. Fermenting the juice
  6. Maturation and bottling

Perry quality depends on the varieties used, with different varieties contributing different characteristics to the final drink.

Conservation Challenges

Perry pear orchards face several challenges:

  • Ancient trees reaching end of lifespan
  • Decline in traditional perry making
  • Development pressure on orchard land
  • Lack of new planting
  • Disease and pests (particularly pear scab)

GOT's Perry Pear Work

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust works to conserve perry pears through:

  • Surveying and documenting traditional perry orchards
  • Identifying and preserving perry pear varieties
  • Supporting traditional perry makers
  • Promoting new perry pear planting
  • Raising awareness of perry heritage
  • Training in perry pear management

Growing Perry Pears

If you're interested in growing perry pears:

  • Choose varieties suited to your location
  • Perry pears need space - they grow large
  • Be patient - trees take years to bear significant crops
  • Plant multiple varieties for pollination
  • Consider joining or starting a community perry project

The Perry Revival

There's growing interest in traditional perry:

  • Artisan perry makers reviving traditional methods
  • New perry orchards being planted
  • Protected Geographical Indication status for traditional perry
  • Tourism interest in perry heritage
  • Recognition of perry orchards' environmental value

This revival offers hope for the future of Gloucestershire's perry pear heritage, but continued effort is needed to conserve these remarkable trees and the traditions associated with them.

item.title: Plum Varieties
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Plum Varieties of Gloucestershire

Gloucestershire's Plum Heritage

While less famous than the county's apples and perry pears, plums have also been an important part of Gloucestershire's orchard heritage. The county has several distinctive plum varieties and a tradition of plum growing stretching back centuries.

Types of Plums

Plums grown in Gloucestershire include:

  • Dessert Plums - Sweet varieties for eating fresh
  • Culinary Plums - Cooking and preserving varieties
  • Damsons - Small, tart plums for preserves and flavoring
  • Gages - Sweet, highly-flavored dessert plums
  • Dual Purpose - Varieties suitable for multiple uses

Gloucestershire Plum Varieties

Several plum varieties are associated with Gloucestershire:

Some varieties originated in the county, while others have been grown here for generations and adapted to local conditions.

Download our comprehensive guide: Gloucestershire Plums (PDF)

Notable Gloucestershire Plums

Key varieties include:

  • Pershore Yellow Egg - Though named for nearby Worcestershire, commonly grown in Gloucestershire
  • Victoria - The most popular plum in England, widely grown in the county
  • Severn Cross - Regional variety
  • Local Damsons - Various damson varieties found in hedgerows and orchards
  • Greengage types - Heritage gages in old gardens

Growing Plums in Gloucestershire

Plums generally grow well in the county:

  • Well-suited to the climate
  • Thrive in Gloucestershire's soils
  • Early flowering (risk of frost damage)
  • Generally less demanding than apples
  • Good crops in favorable years

Plum Tree Characteristics

Plum trees have distinctive features:

  • Generally smaller than apple trees
  • Beautiful spring blossom (early flowering)
  • Self-fertile varieties available
  • Start bearing fruit relatively young
  • May need support for heavy crops
  • Susceptible to certain pests and diseases

Harvest and Use

Harvest Season:

Plums ripen from July through September depending on variety:

  • Early varieties - July to early August
  • Mid-season - August
  • Late varieties - September
  • Damsons - typically September to October

Uses:

  • Fresh eating (dessert varieties)
  • Cooking and baking
  • Jams and preserves
  • Chutneys and sauces
  • Freezing for later use
  • Plum wine and liqueurs

Heritage Plum Orchards

Traditional plum orchards in Gloucestershire:

  • Often planted in market garden settings
  • Mixed with other fruit trees
  • Found in cottage gardens and smallholdings
  • Some commercial orchards historically
  • Many old trees surviving in hedgerows

Conservation Challenges

Plum varieties face several conservation issues:

  • Less attention than apples in heritage work
  • Old trees reaching end of life
  • Difficulty identifying some varieties
  • Limited documentation of local varieties
  • Disease pressure (especially bacterial canker)

GOT's Plum Conservation Work

The Gloucestershire Orchard Trust works to conserve plum heritage through:

  • Surveying and documenting plum trees
  • Identifying heritage varieties
  • Recording local plum varieties
  • Encouraging plum planting
  • Preserving grafting material
  • Raising awareness of plum heritage

Growing Heritage Plums

If you're interested in growing traditional plum varieties:

  • Choose varieties suited to your space and purpose
  • Consider both dessert and cooking varieties
  • Self-fertile varieties are easier for small gardens
  • Protect blossom from late frosts if possible
  • Many heritage varieties are excellent for gardens
  • Damsons are particularly hardy and reliable

The Value of Plum Diversity

Preserving diverse plum varieties provides:

  • Range of flavors and uses
  • Extended harvest season
  • Genetic diversity for future breeding
  • Connection to local food heritage
  • Resilience to pests and diseases
  • Cultural and historical value

While they may not be as celebrated as apples or perry pears, plums are an important part of Gloucestershire's orchard heritage that deserves recognition and conservation.
